article_title: Smaller, Younger, and More Impactful: How AI-Assisted Writing Transforms Research Teams
citation: Haoyang Wang, Mingze Zhang, Yi Bu, Star Xing Zhao, Meijun Liu. (2026). Smaller, Younger, and More Impactful: How AI-Assisted Writing Transforms Research Teams. https://openalex.org/
title: Junior-researcher AI adoption account: diffusion of innovations, publish-or-perish incentives, and displacement of senior writing tasks
description: The article offers a three-part explanation for why AI-assisted writing teams are younger. First, drawing on diffusion of innovations theory, it states that "younger individuals tend to be early adopters of new technologies and more open to novel ideas", suggesting junior researchers are more inclined to adopt AI-assisted writing. Second, junior researchers face intense publish-or-perish pressure with limited time and resources, giving them incentives to use tools that speed up research. Third, AI now performs manuscript preparation, editing, and formatting tasks traditionally handled by senior authors, reducing the need for senior involvement and allowing teams to function with fewer senior authors.
requirements: AI-assisted writing tools must be accessible to junior researchers
constraints: The account is the authors' interpretation offered to explain the observed age pattern, not a tested mechanism
target_learners: junior researchers
research teams in science
target_learning_goals: adoption of AI-assisted writing in academic work
career development of early-career scientists
examples: The article cites a large-scale study of over two million scientists in which junior researchers who adopted AI were more likely to become established scientists and saw faster career progression
key_sources: Haoyang Wang, Mingze Zhang, Yi Bu, Star Xing Zhao, Meijun Liu. (2026). Smaller, Younger, and More Impactful: How AI-Assisted Writing Transforms Research Teams. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.27404

article_title: Verified, not generated: expert-verified AI study materials and the distribution of learning gains in a university course
citation: Dang, C. T., & Nguyen, A. (2026). Verified, not generated: expert-verified AI study materials and the distribution of learning gains in a university course.
title: Judgement burden: the expertise and effort a learner must supply to screen AI output before learning from it
description: Judgement burden is a learner-level construct explaining when generative AI narrows versus widens attainment gaps. The article defines it: "the expertise and effort a learner must supply to distinguish usable from unusable AI output before learning from it". It has two components — variability of output quality and the location of responsibility for checking. Where learners must check variable output, gains accrue to those with the knowledge to check it; where checking is done before release, gains accrue to those who lacked that knowledge. It is related to, but distinct from, cognitive load: checking AI output is extraneous load whose source and bearer the construct names.
requirements: AI-generated material whose quality varies, so that someone must check it before it can be trusted for learning
constraints: The article states the design cannot separate verification from the material it accompanied, so the account's screening prediction (unverified release should produce smaller lower-tail gains) is untested in its data
target_learners: first-year university students in a compulsory economics course
target_learning_goals: examination performance in undergraduate economics, particularly for lower-attaining students
examples: The study's deployment moved the burden upstream: a named graduate teaching assistant checked every NotebookLM output against source materials before release under the label "AI-generated and academically verified".
key_sources: Dang, C. T., & Nguyen, A. (2026). Verified, not generated: expert-verified AI study materials and the distribution of learning gains in a university course. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07097

article_title: Learning in a global society
citation: Jan Visser. (2006). Learning in a Global Society. Learning Development Institute. https://www.learndev.org
title: Distance education should be judged by whether it contributes to a better world, not merely by improved access, participation and cost
description: The chapter argues that insofar as distance education strives to overcome the shortcomings of school systems, it should be judged by the standards of Article 26 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, which links education to "the full development of the human personality" and to strengthening respect for human rights and fundamental freedoms. The primary question is therefore not how distance education has improved access and participation and at what cost, but whether it contributes to a better world. This aligns with the UNESCO-convened expert group's recommendation that distance education take a critical look at itself in light of current knowledge about how people learn.
requirements: Willingness to critique established practice against the purposes of education rather than only measures of access and cost-effectiveness
constraints: The author notes the prevailing rhetoric of cost-effectiveness, economies of scale, and parity of esteem has kept thinking about distance education locked in the dominant classroom model
target_learners: distance education practitioners, planners, and educational policymakers
target_learning_goals: education directed toward the full development of the human personality and respect for human rights and fundamental freedoms
examples: The UNESCO-convened group of 23 experts meeting in Karlsruhe recommended that distance education take a critical look at itself, asking how existing experience fits present-day society and current knowledge about how people learn
key_sources: Jan Visser. (2006). Learning in a Global Society. Learning Development Institute. https://www.learndev.org

article_title: Learning to solve ill-defined statistics problems: does self-explanation quality mediate the worked example effect?
citation: Bichler, S., Stadler, M., Bühner, M., Greiff, S., & Fischer, F. (2022). Learning to solve ill-defined statistics problems: does self-explanation quality mediate the worked example effect? Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-022-09579-4
title: Justified-claims coding scheme for self-explanation quality in ill-defined statistics problems
description: The article develops a coding scheme assessing self-explanation quality as the degree to which written problem solutions include correctly applied and justified conceptual information. For each of three problems, three claims (variables and design, statistical analysis, statistical assumptions) were coded as no claim (0), incomplete (0.5), or complete (1), and separately coded for justification (visually, spatially, or verbally linked). Scores were summed to a 0–27 self-explanation quality measure (Cronbach's α = .78), with concept application coded separately to capture the inferences learners made.
requirements: Written artifacts from learners prompted to justify their answers; expert solutions used to identify the claims and justifying information per problem.
constraints: The authors argue this operationalization suits ill-defined problems, justification prompts, written artifacts, and application-oriented knowledge; whether self-explanation quality mediates may depend on how quality is conceptualized and the targeted outcome.
target_learners: university students in psychology, educational science, or school psychology
target_learning_goals: application-oriented knowledge of statistical methods for investigating research problems
examples: A learner suggesting a between-subjects design was coded 0.5 for missing details; a within-subjects suggestion was coded 0 for incorrect; verbal links such as 'consequently' or 'therefore' counted as justification.
key_sources: Bichler, S., Stadler, M., Bühner, M., Greiff, S., & Fischer, F. (2022). Learning to solve ill-defined statistics problems: does self-explanation quality mediate the worked example effect? Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-022-09579-4

article_title: Metacognitive effects of instructional visuals: the role of cue use and judgment type
citation: Jaeger, A. J., & Fiorella, L. (2024). Metacognitive effects of instructional visuals: the role of cue use and judgment type. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-023-09370-x
title: Judgment type moderates how instructional visuals affect metacomprehension through cue utilization
description: The article proposes that the type of metacognitive judgment students are asked to make (test performance, explaining, or drawing) activates different types of cues, which in turn determines how the presence of instructional visuals affects metacomprehension accuracy. Drawing judgments uniquely prompt students to consult visual information, making them especially vulnerable to superficial visual cues when images are present. The framework builds on Koriat's cue utilization framework distinguishing representation-based cues (tied to sensemaking experiences) from heuristic cues (tied to general beliefs about self or materials). The authors state that "Prompting students to judge their ability to generate drawings may encourage students to make greater use of the provided visuals as cues to inform their judgments."
requirements: Learners must make metacognitive judgments after reading expository science texts
Judgment prompts must differ in whether they direct attention to visual representations
constraints: Tested only with undergraduate populations reading biology and chemistry texts
Diagrams were conceptual but not specifically designed to enhance text content
target_learners: undergraduate students in STEM courses
target_learning_goals: accurate metacomprehension monitoring of science text comprehension
examples: Across Studies 1a, 1b, 2, and 3, draw judgments were differentially harmed by image presence compared to test and explain judgments, and visual cues were reported only for draw judgments.
key_sources: Jaeger, A. J., & Fiorella, L. (2024). Metacognitive effects of instructional visuals: the role of cue use and judgment type. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-023-09370-x

article_title: Cracking Chicken-Egg Conundrums: Juxtaposing Contemporaneous and Lagged Reciprocal Effects Models of Academic Self-Concept and Achievement’s Directional Ordering
citation: Marsh, H. W., Guo, J., Pekrun, R., Lüdtke, O., & Núñez-Regueiro, F. (2024). Cracking Chicken-Egg Conundrums: Juxtaposing Contemporaneous and Lagged Reciprocal Effects Models of Academic Self-Concept and Achievement's Directional Ordering. Educational Psychology Review, 36. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09887-w
title: Juxtapose results from competing panel models rather than selecting a single best model by goodness-of-fit
description: The article recommends that longitudinal model evaluation rest on substantive interpretation alongside fit indices, following Muthén and Asparouhov's advice. Because alternative models may be formally equivalent or hard to distinguish by fit, "conclusions should be based on the juxtaposition of different results rather than selecting a single "best" model based on goodness-of-fit" when competing models each support a priori theory-based hypotheses. Researchers should report results from competing models and consider more parsimonious constrained versions when convergence problems arise.
requirements: A priori theory-based hypotheses to differentiate models whose fit is similar, and reporting of results from multiple competing models
constraints: Convergence problems are common in fully reciprocal lag0-plus-lag1 models, so parsimonious versions constraining non-significant parameters may be needed
target_learners: secondary school students
target_learning_goals: valid causal-ordering inference from longitudinal panel data
examples: The article fit CLPM, RI-CLPM, PCPM, RI-CCLPM and lag2 variants to the PALMA data and interpreted them jointly rather than choosing one winner
key_sources: Marsh, H. W., Guo, J., Pekrun, R., Lüdtke, O., & Núñez-Regueiro, F. (2024). Cracking Chicken-Egg Conundrums: Juxtaposing Contemporaneous and Lagged Reciprocal Effects Models of Academic Self-Concept and Achievement's Directional Ordering. Educational Psychology Review, 36. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09887-w

article_title: Inconclusive Evidence for a Prospective Effect of Academic Self-Concept on Achievement: A Simulated Reanalysis and Comment on Marsh et al. (2024)
citation: Kimmo Sorjonen, Bo Melin, Gustav Nilsonne. (2025). Inconclusive Evidence for a Prospective Effect of Academic Self-Concept on Achievement: A Simulated Reanalysis and Comment on Marsh et al. (2024). Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10008-4
title: Test alternative longitudinal models and juxtapose their results and interpretations before drawing causal conclusions
description: The article endorses Marsh et al.'s (2024) recommendation that researchers "test alternative models and juxtapose their results and interpretations". When findings from alternative models converge, causal conclusions are corroborated; when they diverge, "caution is advised and causal conclusions appear premature". The authors demonstrate this by fitting RI-CLPM, LCSM, ESDM and STARTS models to the same simulated data and finding contradictory positive, negative, and null effects.
requirements: Multiple competing longitudinal models fitted to the same data; willingness to withhold causal claims when findings diverge
constraints: The article's demonstration rests on simulated data resembling the original studies, and on observational data from which causality is difficult, maybe impossible, to infer
target_learners: secondary school students
target_learning_goals: academic self-concept
academic achievement
examples: The authors fitted four (and two additional modified) models to simulated PALMA-like data and validated the divergence on simulated TRAIN-like data, concluding that claims of reciprocal causal effects appear premature
key_sources: Kimmo Sorjonen, Bo Melin, Gustav Nilsonne. (2025). Inconclusive Evidence for a Prospective Effect of Academic Self-Concept on Achievement: A Simulated Reanalysis and Comment on Marsh et al. (2024). Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10008-4

article_title: Tests for the Measurement of Certain Phases of Linguistic Organization in Sentences.
citation: Greene, H. A. (1928). Tests for the Measurement of Certain Phases of Linguistic Organization in Sentences. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org
title: Jumbled thought-unit exercise design: three to eleven parts, randomized permutations excluding the normal first element, numbered response format
description: Each exercise presents the thought units of a sentence as numbered groups of words in jumbled order; the subject writes the numbers in the proper order, permitting an objective record without rewriting the sentence. Exercises were classified as threes, fours, fives, etc., by number of elements, from three to eleven parts. Number combinations were generated independently of the sentences and paired with exercises at random, excluding arrangements where the element that normally comes first stays first.
requirements: The part that normally comes first in a sentence must not appear first in the exercise, because that made getting started too simple
constraints: Suitable exercises of the more complex type were very hard to secure
target_learners: children in grades three to eight
target_learning_goals: sentence organization ability
examples: The sentence 'The dog saw his shadow in the water' was divided into the dog; saw; his shadow; in the water, and jumbled as saw, in the water, his shadow, the dog with the answer recorded as 4-1-3-2
key_sources: Greene, H. A. (1928). Tests for the Measurement of Certain Phases of Linguistic Organization in Sentences. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org

article_title: Report of the twenty-fourth annual meeting of the American Psychological Association, Chicago, December 28-30, 1915.
citation: Kelley, T. L. (1915). Report of the Twenty-fourth Annual Meeting of the American Psychological Association, Chicago, December 28-30, 1915. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.jstor.org/journal/jeducpsych
title: Judd's thesis that general psychology fails to ground school practice, and that teachers need 'educational psychology' or 'experimental education' instead
description: Judd's framework holds that general psychology, as then taught, does not supply a scientific background for school practice because it is too broad and its internal disputes distract prospective teachers. He argues that "Students do not and can not make the applications" of general psychology to educational situations, so application must be built into the course itself. He proposes "educational psychology," or perhaps better "experimental education," for the rank and file of teachers, while agreeing with Haggerty on the value of general psychology for leaders in educational science.
requirements: A first course must make beginning education students aware of the problems of education and give them specific facts contributing to solving those problems.
constraints: The thesis is presented as an address position at the 1915 meeting, not as a tested result; it applies to courses for prospective teachers rather than to psychology training for research leaders.
target_learners: prospective teachers
beginning education students
target_learning_goals: applying psychological principles to educational situations
understanding problems of education
examples: Haggerty presented the University of Indiana's course of study, including elementary, experimental, educational and other psychology courses, recommended as preparation for advanced research work in education.
key_sources: Kelley, T. L. (1915). Report of the Twenty-fourth Annual Meeting of the American Psychological Association, Chicago, December 28-30, 1915. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.jstor.org/journal/jeducpsych

article_title: Construct-level predictive validity of educational attainment and intellectual aptitude tests in medical student selection: meta-regression of six UK longitudinal studies.
citation: McManus IC, Dewberry Chris, Nicholson Sandra, Dowell Jonathan S, Woolf Katherine, Potts Henry WW. (2013). Construct-level predictive validity of educational attainment and intellectual aptitude tests in medical student selection: meta-regression of six UK longitudinal studies. BMC Medicine. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3827328/
title: Judge selection measures by construct-level predictive validity, not by correlations within the selected group
description: The article argues that a key error in selection research is assessing validity via correlations among those already admitted, which are inevitably depressed by restriction of range and can lead to wrongly concluding that measures like A-level grades are of little value. Instead, selectors should estimate the construct-level predictive validity — the true predictor-outcome correlation applicable to the whole applicant pool — using corrections for range restriction, unreliability and right-censorship. The article demonstrates this with six UK cohorts, showing CLPVs (.450 mean) far exceed raw entrant correlations (.171 mean).
requirements: Data on predictor score distributions in both applicants and entrants, plus reliability estimates for predictors and outcomes
Statistical correction methods (e.g., the MCMC-adapted Hunter-Schmidt-Le approach) to infer the true correlation from entrant data
constraints: Estimates depend on assumptions about underlying distributions; the method can be erroneous for heavily right-censored predictors unless specifically adapted
CLPVs are estimated less reliably than conventional correlations (equivalent N about a quarter of actual N)
target_learners: medical school applicants and admissions selectors in UK and comparable selection contexts
target_learning_goals: accurate evaluation of how well selection measures predict future training performance
examples: The article cites Sir George Smart's 1973 claim that A-level grades had low correlation with medical school performance, and Burt's 1943 'time-honoured fallacy' of judging selection efficiency by order-of-merit prediction within the selected group, as instances of the error the principle corrects
key_sources: McManus IC, Dewberry Chris, Nicholson Sandra, Dowell Jonathan S, Woolf Katherine, Potts Henry WW. (2013). Construct-level predictive validity of educational attainment and intellectual aptitude tests in medical student selection: meta-regression of six UK longitudinal studies. BMC Medicine. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3827328/

article_title: Content Delivery Using Augmented Reality to Enhance Students' Performance in a Building Design and Assembly Project
citation: Arezoo Shirazi and Amir H. Behzadan. (2015). Content Delivery Using Augmented Reality to Enhance Students' Performance in a Building Design and Assembly Project. Advances in Engineering Education. https://advances.asee.org/
title: Mobile AR pedagogical application with virtual instructor avatar and image-based element information (Junaio/AREL-based)
description: A mobile augmented reality application built on Junaio, an open-source web-based AREL programming environment, combining two channel types. A location-based channel placed an AR instructor avatar at a point of interest so students could watch step-by-step instructional videos at their own pace, while "image-base channels were used to attach 2D/3D virtual information to each model building element", delivering material type, weight, cost, and dimensions when students scanned tracking images. It was tested as the test-treatment instruction and information delivery platform in the building design and assembly experiment.
requirements: Students need a mobile device (smartphone or tablet) able to run the AR application and scan QR codes and tracking images
constraints: Only 36% of test-group students found it very easy to retrieve measurement information; 54% needed several rounds of trial and error
Students had to spend upfront time learning how to use the application
target_learners: junior and senior level undergraduate construction and civil engineering students
target_learning_goals: building design and assembly
relating abstract engineering topics to practical scenarios
collaboration and communication skills
examples: In the experiment, test-group students scanned a 2-page handout's QR codes to reach the virtual instructor and scanned tracking images on building elements to retrieve design and performance information
key_sources: Arezoo Shirazi and Amir H. Behzadan. (2015). Content Delivery Using Augmented Reality to Enhance Students' Performance in a Building Design and Assembly Project. Advances in Engineering Education. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1076141

article_title: The Impact of a Junior High School Community Intervention Project: Moving beyond the Testing Juggernaut and into a Community of Creative Learners
citation: Nelson, L. P., McMahan, S. K., & Torres, T. (2012). The Impact of a Junior High School Community Intervention Project: Moving Beyond the Testing Juggernaut and Into a Community of Creative Learners. School Community Journal, 22(1). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ970682
title: Two-year community intervention program built on a 20-partner steering committee
description: A two-year intervention in which a steering committee of 20 community partners — including faculty, parents, students, nonprofits, university representatives, city officials, law enforcement, and businesses — developed activities such as mentoring programs, afterschool clubs, and community events. Its stated goals were to "decrease school absenteeism", increase academic performance, and generate positive relationships that increase students' engagement and excitement about their school and community. Programs included school branding, pep rallies, mural painting, attendance contests, open house/field days, cooking and soccer clubs, and a career readiness program.
requirements: A committed group of community leaders and a cohesive team of adults from the community who generate individual relationships with students
Cooperation of school leadership to sustain the programs
constraints: The study reports that efforts to sustain the positive changes without the cooperation of school leadership were entirely ineffective once administration refocused solely on test scores
target_learners: 7th and 8th grade students in an urban, economically disadvantaged, high-minority junior high school
target_learning_goals: Student engagement and excitement about school
School attendance
Positive perceptions of school climate
examples: The steering committee piloted new projects across two years; the afterschool soccer club was sustained beyond project funding and expanded district-wide
key_sources: Nelson, L. P., McMahan, S. K., & Torres, T. (2012). The Impact of a Junior High School Community Intervention Project: Moving Beyond the Testing Juggernaut and Into a Community of Creative Learners. School Community Journal, 22(1). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ974689

article_title: Length in Listening Texts as a Single Determiner of Difficulty for Comprehension
citation: İlhan, B. (2018). Length in listening texts as a single determiner of difficulty for comprehension. Journal of Language and Linguistic Studies, 14(3), 336-346. https://www.jlls.org
title: Judge listening text difficulty by multiple factors together rather than by length alone
description: Because phasing long texts produced no significant comprehension advantage and students named single-word focus, speech rate, and pronunciation more often than length, the article concludes teachers should not reject texts merely for being long. The author states teachers "should consider the quality of listening texts by considering all these factors together rather than just judging it to be difficult because of its length." Length should be weighed alongside strategies, speech rate, and pronunciation.
requirements: Awareness of students' strategy use, speech-rate tolerance, and pronunciation/intonation challenges when selecting texts
constraints: Findings come from one Turkish university context with B1-level learners and texts of a single genre and topic
target_learners: EFL learners in university preparation classes
target_learning_goals: listening comprehension
appropriate selection of listening texts for practice and assessment
examples: The study divided texts longer than three minutes into phases of one minute and thirty seconds at most and compared comprehension with a control group listening all at once
key_sources: İlhan, B. (2018). Length in listening texts as a single determiner of difficulty for comprehension. Journal of Language and Linguistic Studies, 14(3), 336-346. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1193259

article_title: Perceived School Fairness and Academic Functioning in Early Adolescents: Differential Associations for Adolescents with or Without ADHD?
citation: Martinez, A. C., Green, C. D., Peugh, J. L., & Becker, S. P. (2026). Perceived School Fairness and Academic Functioning in Early Adolescents: Differential Associations for Adolescents with or Without ADHD? Research on Child and Adolescent Psychopathology. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10802-025-01419-6
title: Justice sensitivity as an explanatory account of ADHD students' heightened responses to school (un)fairness
description: The article draws on justice sensitivity — "individual differences in the frequency in which injustice is perceived and the intensity of emotional, cognitive, and behavioral reactions to injustice" — to explain why perceived fairness may matter more for youth with ADHD. Theoretical models propose frequent injustice experiences increase the activation potential of injustice-related concepts, raising justice sensitivity over time. The authors theorize youth with ADHD may develop heightened justice sensitivity from frequent injustice experienced as a by-product of ADHD-related challenges, making them more likely to perceive unfairness and react intensely.
requirements: The account presupposes that students actually encounter injustice experiences in the school setting
constraints: The study did not measure justice sensitivity directly; the account is offered as interpretation, and it is unclear whether lower fairness perceptions reflect actual injustice or misinterpretation of fair environments
target_learners: early adolescents with ADHD
target_learning_goals: understanding how fairness perceptions shape engagement, motivation, and learning problems
examples: The article cites empirical work showing that being confronted with injustice increases state justice sensitivity and that more frequent injustice over six months predicted relative increases in justice sensitivity ratings
key_sources: Martinez, A. C., Green, C. D., Peugh, J. L., & Becker, S. P. (2026). Perceived School Fairness and Academic Functioning in Early Adolescents: Differential Associations for Adolescents with or Without ADHD? Research on Child and Adolescent Psychopathology. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10802-025-01419-6

article_title: Coaching inexperienced clinicians before a high stakes medical procedure: randomized clinical trial.
citation: Flynn Stephen G, Park Raymond S, Jena Anupam B, Staffa Steven J, Kim Samuel Y, Clarke Julia D, Pham Ivy V, Lukovits Karina E, Huang Sheng Xiang, Sideridis Georgios D, Bernier Rachel S, Fiadjoe John E, Weinstock Peter H, Peyton James M, Stein Mary Lyn, Kovatsis Pete G. (2024). Coaching inexperienced clinicians before a high stakes medical procedure: randomized clinical trial. The BMJ. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC11648086/
title: Provide brief expert coaching immediately before a high stakes procedure rather than relying only on intraoperative instruction
description: Just-in-time training brings structured, expert-led rehearsal to minutes or hours before a real clinical performance, adapting practices universal in sports and music to medicine. In this trial it meant a standardized coaching session "on an infant manikin within one hour of patient intubation," covering critical intubation steps and challenge-specific coaching insights. The key principle the authors state is "to bring the time between training and implementation for a procedure much closer together." It improved first attempt success, competency metrics, and cognitive load for inexperienced clinicians.
requirements: A dedicated expert coach or coaching team available near the clinical environment
Equipment and technique for the coaching session matched to the planned clinical approach
A brief, standardized session format flexible enough to correct trainee-specific issues
constraints: Coaching sessions lasted a maximum of 5 to 10 minutes to avoid slowing workflow
Many institutions might lack dedicated simulation suites near clinical environments, though the authors suggest nearby workrooms or the operating or patient room could be used
The trial was single center and non-blinded; the authors call it a proof of principle
target_learners: Inexperienced clinicians: pediatric anesthesia fellows, residents, and student registered nurse anesthetists
target_learning_goals: Procedural skill performance on high stakes clinical procedures such as infant intubation
examples: Treatment trainees completed two successful manikin intubations or 10 minutes of coaching before each patient encounter, with coaching repeated before each of up to five intubations
For emergent procedures with no time for pre-procedure coaching, the authors propose briefly coaching trainees at the start of each shift where such procedures are likely
key_sources: Flynn Stephen G, Park Raymond S, Jena Anupam B, Staffa Steven J, Kim Samuel Y, Clarke Julia D, Pham Ivy V, Lukovits Karina E, Huang Sheng Xiang, Sideridis Georgios D, Bernier Rachel S, Fiadjoe John E, Weinstock Peter H, Peyton James M, Stein Mary Lyn, Kovatsis Pete G. (2024). Coaching inexperienced clinicians before a high stakes medical procedure: randomized clinical trial. The BMJ. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC11648086/

article_title: Analysis of the applicability and utility of a gamified didactics with exergames at primary schools: Qualitative findings from a natural experiment.
citation: Quintas-Hijós Alejandro, Peñarrubia-Lozano Carlos, Bustamante Juan Carlos. (2020). Analysis of the applicability and utility of a gamified didactics with exergames at primary schools: Qualitative findings from a natural experiment. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0231269
title: Just Dance Now exergame with ClassDojo gamification platform and ad hoc Excel game board as the intervention's technological toolkit
description: The intervention's technological toolkit comprised the Just Dance Now exergame (chosen because it can be applied in the facilities of the participating schools and is based on accessible materials: laptop, screen projector, Internet, and smartphone), the ClassDojo virtual platform for contextual gamification with badges and points accumulated and consultable at any time, and an ad hoc digital game board designed in Microsoft Excel where students entered their dance scores. Ten exergame dances were selected from 300 dances on the Just Dance Now web platform based on motor difficulty, cultural variety and adjusting values to Primary Education.
requirements: Wi-Fi connectivity, facilities, laptop, screen projector, Internet, and smartphone
constraints: Wi-Fi signal interruptions at all four schools prevented the exergame activity from continuing
smartphone availability limited devices so some students danced without a phone and could not score points
target_learners: primary school students in Physical Education (grades 5-6, aged 10-12)
target_learning_goals: dance skills
motivation toward Physical Education
examples: Students entered the score of each dance indicated by the Just Dance Now exergame on the gamifier board using a laptop available in class, immediately after dancing each dance during class time
key_sources: Quintas-Hijós Alejandro, Peñarrubia-Lozano Carlos, Bustamante Juan Carlos. (2020). Analysis of the applicability and utility of a gamified didactics with exergames at primary schools: Qualitative findings from a natural experiment. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0231269

article_title: Effectiveness and safety of a laparoscopic training system combined with modified reconstruction techniques for total laparoscopic distal gastrectomy.
citation: Zhang Shun, Orita Hajime, Egawa Hiroyuki, Matsui Ryota, Yamauchi Suguru, Yube Yukinori, Kaji Sanae, Takahashi Toru, Oka Shinichi, Inaki Noriyuki, Fukunaga Tetsu. (2020). Effectiveness and safety of a laparoscopic training system combined with modified reconstruction techniques for total laparoscopic distal gastrectomy. World Journal of Gastroenterology. https://doi.org/10.3748/wjg.v26.i13.1490
title: Four-component laparoscopic gastrectomy training system (Juntendo)
description: A structured surgical education system in which trainees "received systematic education about laparoscopic gastrectomy in four components": (1) understanding anatomy and standard procedures via theoretical study and repeated viewing of non-edited operative videos; (2) mastering basic laparoscopic skills using a training box, computer simulator, and hands-on porcine laboratory sessions; (3) gaining intraoperative experience through simple laparoscopic surgeries and serving as scope operator then assistant; and (4) receiving direction from a trainer acting as first assistant during real TLDG. The study evaluated whether this system enabled safe, feasible trainee performance.
requirements: Trainees complete all four components, including basic skills practice and graduated assisting experience, before operating as TLDG surgeon
constraints: Evaluated retrospectively at a single high-volume centre; trainees were allocated lower-stage patients, which the authors state may have shaped the learning curve
target_learners: trainee gastrointestinal surgeons with at least 7 years of post-graduation surgical experience
target_learning_goals: performing total laparoscopic distal gastrectomy with Billroth I reconstruction safely and independently
examples: Five trainees who completed the system performed 52 of 92 TLDG cases (56.5%) between June 2016 and June 2019 at Juntendo University Hospital

Effectiveness and safety of a laparoscopic training system combined with modified reconstruction techniques for total laparoscopic distal gastrectomy. article_title: Interactional skills training in undergraduate medical education: ten principles for guiding future research.
citation: Sanson-Fisher R, Hobden B, Carey M, Mackenzie L, Hyde L, Shepherd J. (2019). Interactional skills training in undergraduate medical education: ten principles for guiding future research. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-019-1566-2
title: Justify the content of interactional skills training using explicit, accepted principles, prioritising evidence-based practice
description: The article argues that undergraduate interactional skills content should be selected by explicit principles rather than individual opinion or faculty resource availability. It cites UK consensus guidelines proposing four key principles: ethics and law awareness, reflective practice, professionalism, and "the need for evidence-based practice". Principle four is highlighted as particularly important because healthcare provision should be driven by level I evidence, and skills shown to improve patient outcomes should be taught.
requirements: Clear and explicit principles for determining which interactional skills and topics are incorporated into undergraduate medical education
constraints: Currently there is surprisingly little high-quality evidence about the impact of specific interactional skills interventions on patient outcomes, limiting evidence-based selection
target_learners: undergraduate medical students
target_learning_goals: interactional and communication skills relevant to patient outcomes
examples: The article cites a review of breaking bad news training finding only seven relevant studies, of which four were randomized controlled trials, with only one examining the impact of the training on patient outcomes.
key_sources: Sanson-Fisher R, Hobden B, Carey M, Mackenzie L, Hyde L, Shepherd J. (2019). Interactional skills training in undergraduate medical education: ten principles for guiding future research. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-019-1566-2

article_title: Integrating Juggling with Math Lessons: A Randomized Controlled Trial Assessing Effects of Physically Active Learning on Maths Performance and Enjoyment in Primary School Children.
citation: van den Berg V., Singh A.S., Komen A., Hazelebach C., van Hilvoorde I., Chinapaw M.J.M. (2019). Integrating Juggling with Math Lessons: A Randomized Controlled Trial Assessing Effects of Physically Active Learning on Maths Performance and Enjoyment in Primary School Children. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health 16(14): 2452. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph16142452
title: Juggling-math physically active learning program
description: A 5-week program of 20 short lessons integrating juggling with multiplication-table practice. "Experienced educators, each with a background as a physical education teacher, developed and produced 20 instruction videos in which a juggler shortly introduced the juggling exercises and then combined the juggling exercises with the multiplication tables." Children answered sums verbally when catching the ball, with juggling complexity increasing weekly.
requirements: A classroom digital screen to display the instruction videos, hosted on a password-protected webpage
A teacher instruction manual with an overview of the lessons and tips
constraints: Juggling-math lessons were slightly longer (5 to 8 min) than the control lessons (5 min)
The lessons were of light physical activity intensity
target_learners: 10- to 11-year-old primary school children (grade 5)
target_learning_goals: Memorization of multiplication tables 2 to 9
examples: In the trial, 14 classes were randomly assigned to the video-based juggling-math lessons or to sedentary practice of identical sums, both implemented as part of the daily math curriculum
key_sources: van den Berg V., Singh A.S., Komen A., Hazelebach C., van Hilvoorde I., Chinapaw M.J.M. (2019). Integrating Juggling with Math Lessons: A Randomized Controlled Trial Assessing Effects of Physically Active Learning on Maths Performance and Enjoyment in Primary School Children. article_title: Neonatal Intensive Care Unit Boot Camp: A Preparatory Curriculum for Pediatric Residents.
citation: Surcouf JW, Mumphrey CG, Barkemeyer BM, Buis M, Gupta RW, Olister S, Patrick-Esteve J, Rivera D, Zeringue A, Chauvin SW. (2018). Neonatal Intensive Care Unit Boot Camp: A Preparatory Curriculum for Pediatric Residents. MedEdPORTAL. https://doi.org/10.15766/mep_2374-8265.10720
title: Just-in-time preparatory boot camp: three 1-hour sessions immediately before a high-stakes clinical rotation
description: A recurring monthly curriculum of three 1-hour sessions—two interactive lectures with case-based application and one high-fidelity simulation session—completed 1–2 months before a rotation. The article states it "is designed for just-in-time learning and hands-on practice, that is, immediately prior to starting a rotation," with small groups of two to five residents for individualized support. Sessions cover labs, vital signs, X-rays, nutrition calculations, respiratory management, and on-call problems.
requirements: Residents preview handouts one week prior so sessions can remain active and hands-on
Faculty protected time and detailed faculty notes to maintain consistency across rotating teachers
Access to an on-site high-fidelity simulator
constraints: Covering material in 1-hour intervals is difficult with inexperienced residents; the camp can be expanded to four sessions
Scheduling conflicts can reduce participation; residents may sign up at most 2 months in advance to preserve just-in-time proximity
Debriefing quality depends on group dynamics; inexperienced groups need more scenario and debriefing time
target_learners: pediatric and combined internal medicine/pediatric residents beginning an NICU rotation
target_learning_goals: recognizing and managing common NICU problems and emergencies
interpreting labs, blood gases, and X-rays
nutrition and fluid calculations
basic respiratory support and ventilation management
examples: At LSU Health Sciences Center New Orleans, 57 residents completed the camp from 2014–2017, with sessions scheduled during morning report for attendance credit
key_sources: Surcouf JW, Mumphrey CG, Barkemeyer BM, Buis M, Gupta RW, Olister S, Patrick-Esteve J, Rivera D, Zeringue A, Chauvin SW. (2018). Neonatal Intensive Care Unit Boot Camp: A Preparatory Curriculum for Pediatric Residents. MedEdPORTAL. https://doi.org/10.15766/mep_2374-8265.10720

article_title: Technology in postgraduate medical education: a dynamic influence on learning?
citation: Bullock A, Webb K. (2015). Technology in postgraduate medical education: a dynamic influence on learning? Postgraduate Medical Journal 91(1081):646-650. https://doi.org/10.1136/postgradmedj-2014-132809
title: Judge the educational value of technology by its content and purpose, not by the technology per se
description: The article argues that because technology is often used in combination with other learning tools, its value "is bound to content and purpose" and "needs to be judged on its appropriateness to purpose: what is it being used for and why?". Neither Twitter, YouTube nor apps can be credited or dismissed wholesale without knowing the 'why' of use.
requirements: Value judgements about a technology must be made against the purpose of use, since value "needs to be judged on its appropriateness to purpose: what is it being used for and why?"
constraints: Technology is often used in combination with other learning tools or activities, making its place and value difficult to judge
Technology is an aid to but not a replacement for real workplace experience with patients and should not be judged as if it were a substitute for that contact
target_learners: postgraduate medical trainees
experienced practitioners
target_learning_goals: workplace learning
clinical expertise development
safe and effective patient care
examples: The article notes the value of a YouTube video for enhancing learning cannot be judged on face value as it depends on the content and purpose of the learner's engagement, and that apps should not be dismissed as having limited educational worth without knowing something about purpose
key_sources: Bullock A, Webb K. (2015). Technology in postgraduate medical education: a dynamic influence on learning? Postgraduate Medical Journal 91(1081):646-650. https://doi.org/10.1136/postgradmedj-2014-132809
